stem: A 74-year-old woman comes in worried because she misplaces her keys and sometimes forgets a neighbor's name, which she recalls later. She lives alone, manages her bills and cooking, drives, and works part-time at a florist. Her mood is good. Cognitive screening and the neurologic examination are normal.
oneliner: 74F + misplaces keys, recalls later + independent ADLs/IADLs + good mood + normal cognitive screen → ? → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Order an MRI of the brain
options.B: Refer her to a neurologist
options.C: Start donepezil therapy
options.D: Reassure her that this is normal aging
options.E: Order formal neuropsychological testing

whyNot.A: Imaging is for **focal signs or functional decline**; she has neither
whyNot.B: Specialist referral is not needed when **function and testing are normal**
whyNot.C: Cholinesterase inhibitors are for **diagnosed dementia**, not normal aging
whyNot.E: Formal testing is reserved for **abnormal screening** or functional change

answer: Reassure her that mild forgetfulness is normal with aging
why: She has **intact ADLs and IADLs**, **normal mood**, and **normal cognitive screening**, and recalls forgotten items later. This is **normal age-related forgetfulness**, so reassurance without further workup is correct.

idea.rule: Normal aging spares function and cognitive testing; dementia impairs daily function.
also: Mild cognitive impairment: abnormal testing, ADLs intact
Dementia: decline in ADLs/IADLs plus impaired testing
Depression can mimic memory loss (pseudodementia)
Delirium: acute onset with fluctuating attention

stem: A 55-year-old woman with early breast cancer has been told that lumpectomy with radiation and mastectomy give equal survival. She says, "I cannot decide. What would you do?"
oneliner: 55F + early breast cancer + two equal options + asks "What would you do?" → ? → ?
ask: Which of the following statements is most appropriate?

options.A: "Tell me what you know about each option and what matters to you."
options.B: "This is your decision to make, and I should not influence it."
options.C: "Most women in your situation end up choosing the mastectomy."
options.D: "I would choose the lumpectomy, so I suggest you do the same."
options.E: "I will refer you to a surgeon who can decide with you."

whyNot.B: Refusing to help **abandons** a patient who asked for guidance
whyNot.C: Citing what others choose offers **no individual guidance** and may pressure her
whyNot.D: Giving a personal pick **before** knowing her values substitutes your preferences for hers
whyNot.E: A referral **defers** the conversation and the first step is still unexplored

answer: Explore her understanding and values first
why: When a patient asks for advice among valid options, the first step is to **explore her understanding** of each option and **what matters to her**. This is **shared decision-making**; recommendations come after her values are known.

idea.rule: Before advising, explore the patient's understanding and values.
also: Ask open-ended questions before giving information
Elicit the patient's goals in end-of-life choices
Check understanding with teach-back
Respect autonomy while still offering a recommendation

stem: A 60-year-old man is scheduled for cardiac catheterization. The intern asked to obtain his consent has never watched or read about the procedure and would not be able to answer questions about its risks or alternatives.
oneliner: 60M + cardiac catheterization + intern asked to get consent has never seen the procedure → ? → ?
ask: What is the intern's most appropriate action?

options.A: Have the nurse obtain the patient's signature
options.B: Explain only the most serious risk and request a signature
options.C: Ask the attending physician to obtain the informed consent
options.D: Obtain the signature and defer questions to the cardiologist
options.E: Read the consent form aloud and answer questions from its text

whyNot.A: A nurse witnessing a signature is **not** disclosing risks, benefits and alternatives
whyNot.B: **Partial disclosure** does not meet the standard for informed consent
whyNot.D: A signature given **before** full disclosure and questions is not informed consent
whyNot.E: Reading the form does not replace **knowledgeable discussion** and answering questions

answer: Ask the attending physician, who knows the procedure, to obtain consent
why: Informed consent requires **full disclosure of risks, benefits and alternatives** and the ability to **answer questions**. Someone **unfamiliar** with the procedure cannot do this, so the intern should hand the task to a physician who is.

idea.rule: Consent is valid only if the person obtaining it can explain the procedure.
also: Disclose risks, benefits, alternatives and the option of no treatment
The patient must be competent and act voluntarily
The treating physician, not a witness, carries the duty to inform
A signed form without discussion is not informed consent

stem: A 10-year-old girl arrives unconscious after a car crash with falling blood pressure and free fluid in the abdomen on ultrasound. Both parents are traveling abroad and cannot be reached despite repeated attempts. She needs immediate surgery.
oneliner: 10F + unconscious after crash + internal bleeding + parents unreachable → ? → ?
ask: What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Wait until a parent can be reached by phone
options.B: Obtain a court order before operating
options.C: Ask her teacher to give consent
options.D: Ask the ethics committee to approve surgery first
options.E: Proceed with emergency surgery without parental consent

whyNot.A: Waiting risks **death**; delay is not justified in a life-threatening emergency
whyNot.B: A court order takes **time she does not have**
whyNot.C: A teacher has **no legal authority** to consent for her
whyNot.D: An ethics review is **not required** and would cause fatal delay

why: A life-threatening emergency in an **incapacitated minor** with **unreachable parents** falls under the **emergency exception** (implied consent). The physician treats immediately and documents the circumstances.

idea.rule: In a true emergency, treat first: consent is implied.
also: Unresponsive adult with no surrogate available
Delay would risk death or serious harm
Document why consent could not be obtained
Does not apply to non-urgent care

stem: A 2-day-old girl has trisomy 13 with a severe heart defect, and the parents have chosen comfort-focused care. She cannot suck effectively and cries every few hours, settling each time after a tube feed.
oneliner: 2-day-old F + trisomy 13 + comfort care + cries when hungry, settles after tube feeds → ? → ?
ask: Which approach to feeding is most appropriate?

options.A: Withhold feeding because the diagnosis is lethal
options.B: Give tube feedings whenever she shows hunger
options.C: Offer oral feeding only, without a tube
options.D: Feed to meet the full caloric needs for her age
options.E: Place a gastrostomy tube for long-term feeding

whyNot.A: Her crying is **relieved by feeds**, so withholding them adds suffering
whyNot.C: She **cannot suck**, so oral-only feeding leaves hunger untreated
whyNot.D: Feeding to full caloric targets is **not the aim** of comfort care
whyNot.E: A long-term tube is an **invasive procedure** that does not serve comfort

answer: Tube feeding as needed to relieve hunger (comfort)
why: With a **lethal diagnosis**, the goal is **comfort**. Feeding relieves her hunger distress, so it is **given as needed**, but it is **not pushed** to normal caloric goals or escalated with invasive devices.

idea.rule: In comfort care, give what relieves distress and no more.
also: Pain relief is given even if it may blunt breathing
Treatments that only prolong dying may be withheld
Hunger and thirst relief is part of comfort
Parents decide for the infant within the best-interest standard

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought in by his mother, who is worried that he is too short. His height and weight are near the 40th percentile and he is Tanner stage 4. Examination is normal. The mother looks anxious.
oneliner: 17M + mother worried he is short + normal height, Tanner 4 + anxious parent → ? → ?
ask: What should the physician say first?

options.A: "We will check his hormone levels."
options.B: "He is not going to be any taller."
options.C: "You should accept him as he is."
options.D: "What worries you most about his height?"
options.E: "He is average for his height and weight."

whyNot.A: Testing is premature before her **concern is understood** and his growth is normal
whyNot.B: It is **inaccurate**: Tanner 4 means he may still grow, and it closes the conversation
whyNot.C: It **dismisses** her feelings instead of addressing them
whyNot.E: Facts alone, **before** exploring her worry, may not reassure her

answer: Open-ended question inviting her to explain her concern
why: Before reassuring or testing, **explore the parent's concern** with an **open-ended statement**. His growth is **normal**, but the mother's specific worry is not yet known.

idea.rule: Start with an open-ended question to elicit the concern.
also: Use silence and facilitation to let patients talk
Ask about the patient's understanding before explaining
Reflect emotions before offering facts
Avoid closed questions at the start of the visit

stem: A 52-year-old man tells his primary physician that his cardiologist hurries through visits and ignores his questions. He has had no complications and has not raised this with the cardiologist.
oneliner: 52M + complains cardiologist rushes visits and ignores questions + no harm + not yet discussed with him → ? → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Encourage him to discuss his concerns directly with the cardiologist
options.B: Explain how to file a complaint with the state licensing board
options.C: Call the cardiologist to report the complaint yourself
options.D: Tell him that rushed visits are not unusual these days
options.E: Give him a copy of a patient bill of rights

whyNot.B: Formal complaints are for **serious misconduct**; no harm has occurred
whyNot.C: Calling for him acts **without his permission** and bypasses his own voice
whyNot.D: This **dismisses** his concern and avoids helping him
whyNot.E: A document does not help him **address the problem** directly

answer: Encourage direct discussion with the cardiologist
why: There is **no safety issue** and he has **not yet spoken** to the cardiologist, so the best step is to encourage **direct communication** with that physician. This builds his self-advocacy.

idea.rule: Direct communication is the first step in a non-urgent complaint.
also: Do not criticize colleagues to patients
Report only when patient safety is at risk
Support patient advocacy without taking sides
Avoid acting on the patient's behalf without permission

stem: A 38-year-old woman who speaks only French comes for a gynecologic visit with her 15-year-old daughter, who is bilingual. The patient says she is happy for her daughter to interpret. She needs a sexual history and a pelvic examination for vaginal discharge.
oneliner: 38F + French only + teen daughter offers to interpret + sensitive sexual history → ? → ?
ask: Which of the following statements is most appropriate?

options.A: "Your daughter can interpret, and then she will step out for the examination."
options.B: "How much experience does your daughter have with interpreting?"
options.C: "I will arrange a professional medical interpreter for your visit."
options.D: "Since you prefer your daughter, we will go ahead with her help."
options.E: "We will manage with gestures and simple English."

whyNot.A: A child hearing a **sexual history** risks **inaccurate and incomplete** answers
whyNot.B: Experience does not remove **confidentiality and accuracy** concerns for family members
whyNot.D: Patient preference does not override the need for **qualified interpretation**
whyNot.E: Gestures lead to **errors and missed history**

why: With **limited English proficiency**, a **professional medical interpreter** gives accurate, confidential translation. **Family members**, especially a minor, should not interpret a **sensitive history**.

idea.rule: Use professional interpreters, not family members.
also: Telephone or video interpreters count as professional
Family may be used only in emergencies when no interpreter exists
Address the patient, not the interpreter
Interpreters are bound by confidentiality

stem: A 45-year-old man has been waiting 40 minutes past his appointment time. He is visibly annoyed as the physician enters the room.
oneliner: 45M + physician 40 minutes late + patient visibly annoyed → ? → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate statement?

options.A: "The emergency department kept me busy this morning."
options.B: "Let's move quickly; this visit will not take long."
options.C: "Would you like to reschedule for another day?"
options.D: "My schedule is very tight today, I'm afraid."
options.E: "I'm sorry I kept you waiting; I know your time is valuable."

whyNot.A: Giving a reason without an apology sounds like an **excuse**
whyNot.B: Rushing the visit tells him his concerns are **unimportant**
whyNot.C: It offers no apology and **pushes him out** after he has waited
whyNot.D: It shifts attention to the **physician's problems** rather than his inconvenience

why: The best response is a **direct apology** that **acknowledges the patient's inconvenience** without excuses. This shows respect and eases his frustration.

idea.rule: Apologize and acknowledge; do not make excuses.
also: Acknowledge the patient's emotion
Take responsibility for errors and delays
Avoid defensive explanations
Show empathy before moving to the agenda

stem: A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed lymphoma is about to start chemotherapy. His oncologist offers to go over the side effects, but he says, 'I trust you, just do what is best for me and skip the details.' He is alert, understands his diagnosis, and shows no sign of pressure from anyone.
oneliner: 68M + lymphoma + chemo + competent + declines details voluntarily → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Review every risk with him before starting anyway
options.B: Honor his wish, document it, and offer details later
options.C: Ask his daughter to give consent in his place
options.D: Delay chemotherapy until he agrees to listen
options.E: Obtain a court order before starting treatment

whyNot.A: He has **explicitly declined**; forcing information ignores that choice
whyNot.C: He is **competent**, so no surrogate is needed
whyNot.D: **Delay harms him** and is not required
whyNot.E: A court is for patients who **lack capacity** and no surrogate, not for a waiver

answer: Honor the waiver and document it
why: A **competent** patient may **waive** the right to detailed information, and the physician can honor that **voluntary** wish. Documenting the waiver and keeping the door open to questions completes the plan.

idea.rule: A competent patient can waive information, but cannot be forced to hear it.
also: Therapeutic privilege is rarely allowed and is narrow
Consent must be voluntary and informed
Emergency exception when the patient cannot consent
Patient may name someone else to receive information

stem: A 72-year-old woman with mild dementia declines a recommended hip operation after a fall. Her son asks whether she is even allowed to decide. She explains that surgery would help her walk, says she fears the recovery, and states the same choice repeatedly.
oneliner: 72F + mild dementia + refuses hip surgery + family questions her ability → how to settle?
ask: What is the most appropriate way to determine whether she can decide?

options.A: Request a court ruling on her competence
options.B: Obtain a mandatory psychiatry consultation
options.C: Accept the dementia diagnosis as proof of incapacity
options.D: Assess her capacity for this decision at the bedside
options.E: Let her son decide because of her age

whyNot.A: A court rules on legal **competence**; the bedside question of capacity needs no judge
whyNot.B: Psychiatry may **help in hard cases**, but any treating physician can assess capacity
whyNot.C: A diagnosis of **mild dementia does not remove capacity**; it is judged per decision
whyNot.E: **Age** alone never removes decision-making rights, and her son is not a surrogate while she can decide

why: **Capacity** is **decision-specific** and is judged by the treating physician: does she understand, appreciate, reason and state a choice? She does, so her refusal stands; **competence** is a legal finding made by a court.

idea.rule: Capacity = bedside, per decision, by the physician; competence = legal, by a court.
also: Understand, appreciate, reason, express a choice
Capacity can fluctuate
Mild dementia does not equal incapacity
Minors are presumed to lack legal competence

stem: A 65-year-old man is comatose after a large stroke. He left no advance directive and named no health care proxy. His wife says he would not have wanted prolonged ventilation, while their adult son wants everything done.
oneliner: 65M + coma + no directive or proxy + wife and son disagree → who decides?
ask: Who should make the decision for him?

options.A: His wife
options.B: His adult son
options.C: The attending physician
options.D: The hospital ethics committee
options.E: A court-appointed guardian

whyNot.B: Adult children come **after the spouse**
whyNot.C: The physician does not decide alone when a **surrogate is available**
whyNot.D: The committee only **advises** if the surrogate dispute cannot be resolved
whyNot.E: A guardian is needed only if **no suitable surrogate** exists or conflict is unresolvable

why: Without a directive or proxy, the surrogate order is **spouse, then adult children, then parents, then siblings**. The wife decides using **substituted judgment**: what he would have wanted.

idea.rule: Surrogate order: spouse, adult children, parents, siblings; use substituted judgment.
also: Health care proxy overrides the usual order
Best interest standard if wishes are unknown
Ethics committee advises in unresolved conflict
Court guardian if no surrogate exists

stem: A 16-year-old girl comes to clinic alone and asks to be tested for sexually transmitted infections after unprotected intercourse. She has no symptoms and asks that her parents not be told.
oneliner: 16F + alone + requests STI testing + wants parents not told → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Require parental consent before testing
options.B: Call her parents to inform them
options.C: Test her and keep the visit confidential
options.D: Refuse testing until she is 18
options.E: Refer to a court for permission

whyNot.A: Minors can **consent alone** for this care
whyNot.B: Breaks **confidentiality** without a safety reason
whyNot.D: **Withholding care** harms her and the public
whyNot.E: A court is **not needed** for this service

why: Minors may consent **without parents** for **STI testing and treatment**, contraception, prenatal care and substance-use treatment. She is tested and her **confidentiality** is kept.

idea.rule: Minors consent alone for STIs, contraception, prenatal care, substance use (state rules vary).
also: Emancipated minors decide like adults
Abortion rules vary by state
Emergency care does not need parental consent
Reportable infections still go to public health

stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought in after a car crash with a ruptured spleen. He is pale, tachycardic and hypotensive, and the surgeon says he needs a transfusion now. His parents refuse blood because of their religion.
oneliner: 6M + crash + hemorrhage + needs transfusion + parents refuse on religious grounds → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Respect the parents' refusal
options.B: Wait for a court order
options.C: Give only IV fluids
options.D: Ask the child to decide
options.E: Give the transfusion now

whyNot.A: Parents **cannot refuse life-saving treatment** for a child
whyNot.B: Delay costs the child's life; **emergencies** allow treatment first
whyNot.C: This is a **half-measure** that cannot replace blood
whyNot.D: A 6-year-old **cannot decide**

why: In a **life-threatening emergency**, the physician **treats the child**; parents cannot refuse life-saving care for him. A court order can be sought afterward if time allows, but treatment is not delayed.

idea.rule: Child in danger: treat first; parental refusal does not apply to life-saving care.
also: Parents may refuse for themselves, not for their child
Non-emergent refusals may need a court order
Child abuse concerns are reported
Emergency exception applies without consent

stem: A 41-year-old man tells his psychiatrist he will shoot his former boss tomorrow morning. He says he bought a handgun yesterday and knows where the boss parks.
oneliner: 41M + threat to kill former boss tomorrow + bought a gun → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Keep the information confidential
options.B: Warn the former boss and notify the police
options.C: Document the statement and take no other step
options.D: Increase his medication dose
options.E: Schedule a follow-up visit next week

whyNot.A: Confidentiality **yields** to a credible threat
whyNot.C: Documenting alone **does not protect** the victim
whyNot.D: Treatment does not remove the **imminent danger**
whyNot.E: A visit next week comes **after the threat**

answer: Warn the victim and notify police
why: A **credible threat** to an **identifiable person**, with the means in hand, creates a **duty to protect** (Tarasoff). The physician must warn the person and/or notify the police.

idea.rule: Credible threat + identifiable victim: warn and notify police, even breaking confidentiality.
also: Child abuse must be reported
Reportable infections go to public health
Suicidal intent allows protective steps
Impaired driving risk may be reported in some states

stem: A 58-year-old man had a prostate biopsy yesterday. His adult son phones the clinic and asks the physician for the result. The father has full capacity and has not given permission to share anything.
oneliner: 58M + biopsy result + adult son phones for it + no permission given → response?
ask: Which is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Give the son the biopsy result
options.B: Share only the reassuring parts
options.C: Tell the son but ask him to keep quiet
options.D: Decline, and offer to ask the father first
options.E: Fax the pathology report to the son

whyNot.A: Needs **the patient's permission** first
whyNot.B: Partial disclosure is still **disclosure**
whyNot.C: Asking for **silence** does not make the disclosure acceptable
whyNot.E: Sending the report is **disclosure without consent**

why: A **competent** adult's information belongs to him. Without his **permission**, the physician does not share the result with family and can instead offer to ask the father.

idea.rule: No disclosure to family without a competent patient's permission.
also: HIPAA protects identifiable health information
Patient may name who can receive information
Exceptions: public health reporting, threats, abuse
Surrogate gets information when patient lacks capacity

stem: A 27-year-old man is diagnosed with primary syphilis, shown by a painless penile chancre with positive treponemal and RPR tests. He begs the physician not to tell anyone and refuses to let the health department be told.
oneliner: 27M + new syphilis + asks that it not be reported → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Treat him and report the case to public health
options.B: Treat him and honor his wish not to report
options.C: Treat him and notify his employer
options.D: Report only after he gives written consent
options.E: Report only if he returns with new symptoms

whyNot.B: Reporting a **notifiable infection** is **required by law** and his refusal does not change it
whyNot.C: The employer has **no right** to the information
whyNot.D: Reporting **does not depend on consent**
whyNot.E: Reporting is for **diagnosis**, not for later symptoms

why: Syphilis is a **reportable infection**, so the physician treats him and must report it to public health **without the patient's consent**. Confidentiality is otherwise preserved, and the employer is not told.

idea.rule: Reportable infections go to public health regardless of consent: TB, syphilis, gonorrhea, HIV, hepatitis.
also: Treat and encourage partner notification
The health department can notify partners without naming the patient
Confidentiality is limited by law
Child and elder abuse are also mandatory reports

stem: An 80-year-old woman is brought in unconscious with respiratory failure. Her chart holds a signed living will, written when she was lucid, refusing intubation. Her daughter demands that she be intubated.
oneliner: 80F + unconscious + living will refuses intubation + daughter demands it → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Intubate as the daughter asks
options.B: Ask an ethics committee to override the directive
options.C: Follow the living will and do not intubate
options.D: Obtain a court order first
options.E: Intubate until the family agrees

whyNot.A: The **patient's directive** outranks family wishes
whyNot.B: The committee **cannot override** a valid directive
whyNot.D: A court is **not needed** for a clear, valid directive
whyNot.E: The family's agreement is **not required**

why: A valid **advance directive** written with capacity is **followed even when family disagrees**. The patient's own prior wishes come before the daughter's.

idea.rule: Valid advance directive > surrogate > family wishes.
also: Health care proxy acts when no directive covers the situation
Directive can be revoked by a competent patient
Substituted judgment guides surrogates
Out-of-hospital DNR forms exist

stem: An 88-year-old man with a valid DNR order is admitted with fever, cough and a right lower lobe consolidation. He is alert and stable, and he wants the infection treated.
oneliner: 88M + DNR order + new pneumonia → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Withhold antibiotics because of the DNR
options.B: Switch to comfort care only
options.C: Transfer him to hospice care
options.D: Rescind the DNR order before treating
options.E: Give antibiotics and keep the DNR

whyNot.A: DNR covers **arrest only**; other indicated treatment goes on
whyNot.B: He **wants treatment**; comfort-only care does not match
whyNot.C: Not requested, and **not required** by a DNR
whyNot.D: The DNR is **still valid** and he has not changed it

why: A **DNR order** means **no CPR at cardiopulmonary arrest**. All other indicated treatments, such as **antibiotics** for his pneumonia, continue, and he wants them.

idea.rule: DNR = no CPR at arrest; everything else indicated still proceeds.
also: Do not intubate (DNI) is a separate order
A competent patient can revoke a DNR at any time
Comfort-only care is a separate choice by the patient
DNR is not do-not-treat

stem: A 59-year-old woman returns to clinic with her husband to hear her biopsy result, which shows ovarian cancer. The physician has a private room, sits down, and has the pathology report in hand.
oneliner: 59F + biopsy shows ovarian cancer + setting prepared → first statement?
ask: Which statement should the physician make first?

options.A: 'The biopsy shows ovarian cancer.'
options.B: 'What is your understanding of why we did the biopsy?'
options.C: 'Let me first describe the treatment options for you.'
options.D: 'About half of women with this live five years.'
options.E: 'I would like your husband to tell you the result.'

whyNot.A: The diagnosis comes **after** assessing her understanding
whyNot.C: Treatment comes **after** diagnosis and her readiness
whyNot.D: Prognosis comes **later**, if she wants it
whyNot.E: The physician must **tell the patient personally**

why: In the SPIKES approach, after the **setting**, the next step is **perception**: ask what she already understands. Then ask how much she wants to know before giving the news.

idea.rule: SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Summary.
also: Invitation: ask how much she wants to know
Knowledge: give the news in plain words
Emotions: respond with empathy
Strategy and summary close the visit

stem: A 75-year-old woman has a biopsy showing pancreatic cancer. Her son asks the physician not to tell her, saying it will crush her. She is alert, makes her own decisions, and has not asked to be spared details.
oneliner: 75F + cancer diagnosis + son asks not to tell her → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Agree to keep the diagnosis from her for now
options.B: Tell the son and not the patient
options.C: Tell her the results are still pending
options.D: Explore his fears, then ask her how much to share
options.E: Refer the family to the ethics committee now

whyNot.A: She has a **right to the information**
whyNot.B: She is the **patient** and is competent; the son has no right to her result first
whyNot.C: This is a **lie**
whyNot.E: The issue can be **resolved at the bedside** first

answer: Explore reasons, then ask the patient
why: Family requests for nondisclosure should be **explored**, but the **competent patient** has the right to know. Asking her **how much she wants to know** respects her choice.

idea.rule: Competent patient first: explore family fears, but do not conceal the diagnosis.
also: Patient may waive information
Cultural beliefs are explored respectfully
Never lie to the patient
Use interpreters, not family, for language

stem: A 63-year-old man on a medical ward received a double dose of heparin overnight because of a pump programming error. He has no bleeding, and his aPTT has returned to range by morning.
oneliner: 63M + double heparin dose from pump error + no bleeding yet → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Say nothing because no harm occurred
options.B: Inform only his family about the error
options.C: Disclose the error to him and apologize
options.D: Report it to the nurse manager only
options.E: Tell him only if harm develops later

whyNot.A: Errors that reach the patient **must be disclosed** even without harm
whyNot.B: The **patient** is told first
whyNot.D: Internal reporting is needed but **does not replace disclosure**
whyNot.E: Disclosure **should not wait** for harm

why: An error that **reached the patient** is disclosed **honestly**, with an **apology** and an explanation of what is being done, **even if no harm resulted**. Internal reporting happens in addition.

idea.rule: Disclose errors that reach the patient: facts, apology, prevention plan; also report internally.
also: Near misses are reported internally
Many states have apology laws protecting expressions of sympathy
Disclose to the patient, not just family
Document the event factually

stem: A resident at a teaching hospital is offered several items by a pharmaceutical representative after a lunch talk.
oneliner: Resident + drug rep offers items → which gift may be accepted?
ask: Under AMA guidance, which item may the resident accept?

options.A: A clinical pharmacology textbook
options.B: A paid weekend at a resort
options.C: Cash for attending the talk
options.D: Store gift cards for personal use
options.E: A fee for each prescription written

whyNot.B: **Trips and luxury** gifts are not allowed
whyNot.C: **Cash** is not acceptable
whyNot.D: **Gift cards** are personal benefits
whyNot.E: A payment **tied to prescribing** is unethical

why: Small gifts with **patient or educational benefit**, like a **textbook**, may be accepted. **Cash, trips and anything tied to prescribing** may not.

idea.rule: Accept only small educational or patient-benefit gifts; no cash, trips or prescribing strings.
also: Items should primarily benefit patients or education
Sponsored education should be independent of the company
Disclose conflicts of interest
Gifts must not influence prescribing

stem: A 38-year-old woman is under general anesthesia for an elective cholecystectomy. The resident scrubbing in smells alcohol on the attending surgeon's breath, and he has slurred speech and unsteady hands as he picks up the scalpel.
oneliner: 38F + anesthetized for cholecystectomy + attending smells of alcohol → action?
ask: Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Say nothing and assist with the case
options.B: Stop the operation and alert a supervisor
options.C: Speak with him privately after the case
options.D: Report him to the state licensing board
options.E: Inform the patient when she wakes up

whyNot.A: The patient's **safety is at risk** now
whyNot.C: Waiting lets him **operate impaired**
whyNot.D: A board report **does not stop this operation**; the immediate step is the supervisor
whyNot.E: She is **anesthetized**; telling her later does not stop the harm

why: An **impaired colleague** puts the patient at risk, so the resident must **stop the operation** and alert a **supervisor** (chief of surgery or department head). Referral to the physician health program or licensing board follows later.

idea.rule: Impaired colleague: protect the patient first, then report through the supervisor or health program.
also: A sleep-deprived or ill colleague is also removed from care
Physician health programs support rehabilitation
Reporting an impaired colleague is a duty
Document the observations

stem: A 50-year-old man who smokes tells his physician he wants to quit within the next month. He has not yet chosen a day or a method.
oneliner: 50M + smoker + wants to quit within a month + no plan yet → best next step?
ask: What is the best next step?

options.A: List pros and cons of smoking with him
options.B: Give him more information on its harms
options.C: Wait until he decides on his own
options.D: Congratulate him on maintaining abstinence
options.E: Help him set a quit date and a concrete plan

whyNot.A: Fits **contemplation**; he is past weighing
whyNot.B: He already knows; **information** is not the need
whyNot.C: He **has decided**; waiting wastes the moment
whyNot.D: He has **not quit yet**, so maintenance does not apply

answer: Set a quit date and plan
why: Planning to quit within a month is the **preparation** stage. The best step is to help him choose a **quit date** and a **concrete plan** such as counseling and medication.

idea.rule: Match advice to stage: preparation = quit date and plan.
also: Contemplation: weigh pros and cons
Precontemplation: raise awareness
Action: support and prevent relapse
Maintenance: relapse prevention
